claim: 285 samples were taken from a planar section of a hepatocellular carcinoma of diameter 35mm analyzed by Ling et al., 2015.
source: In Ling et al., 2015, 285 samples of a planar section of a hepatocellular carcinoma of diameter 35mm were taken and analyzed.
evidence: Direct statement from the manuscript describing the dataset.

claim: Each sample in the Ling et al., 2015 study consisted of about 20,000 cells.
source: Each sample consisted of about 20,000 cells (Ling et al., 2015) determined by cell counting.
evidence: Cites Ling et al., 2015 as the source for cell counting data.

claim: 23 samples from the Ling et al., 2015 study were subjected to whole-exome sequencing with average read depth of 74 reads per nucleotide.
source: 23 of these samples were subjected to whole-exome sequencing (average read depth of 74 reads per nucleotide)
evidence: Direct statement about sequencing methodology and depth.

claim: Loci with mutations found in the 23 whole-exome sequenced samples were probed by genotyping in all 285 samples using Sequenom and Sanger sequencing.
source: loci with mutations found in these 23 samples were probed by genotyping (by Sequenom and Sanger sequencing) in all 285 samples (Ling et al., 2015).
evidence: Describes the genotyping methodology applied to the full sample set.

claim: The genotyped data from Ling et al., 2015 consists of 35 mutated loci.
source: The genotyped data consists of 35 mutated loci.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of mutated loci in genotyped data.

claim: Joint variant calling and filtering on all 23 whole-exome samples from Ling et al., 2015 returned 217 mutated loci.
source: Calling variants jointly on all 23 whole-exome samples and filtering as described in Appendix 4.2 returned 217 mutated loci.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of mutated loci after reanalysis.

claim: 169 samples were taken from 11 sections of tumour T1 in the Li et al., 2022 study, with the tumour being approximately 20mm in diameter.
source: 169 samples were taken from 11 sections of tumour T1, which was approximately of 20mm diameter
evidence: Direct statement about sampling and tumour dimensions.

claim: 160 samples were taken from 6 sections of tumour T2 in the Li et al., 2022 study, with the tumour being approximately 15mm in diameter.
source: 160 samples from 6 sections of tumour T2, which was of approximately of 15mm diameter.
evidence: Direct statement about sampling and tumour dimensions.

claim: Each sample in the Li et al., 2022 study consisted of approximately 3200 cells.
source: Each sample consisted of ca. 3200 cells.
evidence: Direct statement about cell count per sample.

claim: 16 samples from T1 and 9 samples from T2 in the Li et al., 2022 study were whole-genome sequenced.
source: 16 (9) samples from T1 (T2) were whole-genome sequenced
evidence: Direct statement about the number of samples subjected to whole-genome sequencing.

claim: Li et al., 2022 reported 906 mutations for T1 and 564 mutations for T2 used for genotyping.
source: Li et al. report 906 (564) mutations used for genotyping of T1 (T2)
evidence: Direct statement citing the number of mutations reported by Li et al.

claim: 563 mutations from T1 and 259 mutations from T2 passed the authors' filters.
source: of which 563 (259) pass our filters.
evidence: Direct statement about the number of mutations passing quality filters.

claim: Under surface growth, offspring clones tend to lie radially outward from their parent clones, leading to a distribution of direction angles centered around zero.
source: Under surface growth, offspring tend to lie radially outward from their parents, leading to a distribution of these direction angles centered around zero.
evidence: Direct statement about the expected distribution under surface growth model.

claim: Under volume growth, cells divide isotropically, leading to a uniform distribution of direction angles.
source: Under volume growth, cells divide isotropically, leading to a uniform distribution of angles.
evidence: Direct statement about the expected distribution under volume growth model.

claim: The empirical data from Ling et al., 2015 show a uniform distribution of the direction angle.
source: The empirical data clearly show a uniform distribution of the direction angle
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 2B showing the distribution.

claim: The empirical data from Ling et al., 2015 show no evidence for radially outward growth caused by faster growth near the edge of the tumour.
source: The empirical data clearly show a uniform distribution of the direction angle, and thus no evidence for radially outward growth caused by faster growth near the edge of the tumour.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from the uniform distribution of direction angles.

claim: Simulations of surface growth show a pronounced maximum at θ=0 in the histogram of direction angles.
source: For surface growth, the histogram of direction angles shows a pronounced maximum at θ=0 produced by the radial outgrowth of clones (Figure 2C)
evidence: Direct statement supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Simulations of volume growth show a flat distribution of direction angles.
source: in a simulation of volume growth, we find a flat distribution (Figure 2D).
evidence: Direct statement supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Under surface growth and neutral evolution, the number of cell divisions since tumorigenesis increases with distance from the tumour centre.
source: Under surface growth and neutral evolution, the number of cell divisions since tumorigenesis, and hence the number of mutations found in a cell, increases with distance from the tumour centre.
evidence: Direct statement about expected pattern under surface growth.

claim: The number of mutations at different distances from the centre in the Ling et al., 2015 data is compatible with volume growth.
source: we find that the number of mutations at different distances from the centre is compatible with volume growth (see Appendix 3—figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to supporting figure.

claim: The dataset of Li et al., 2022 with three-dimensional sampling shows the signature of volume growth in the distribution of direction angles.
source: Similarly, the dataset of Li et al., 2022 with three-dimensional sampling also shows the signature of volume growth, both in the distribution of direction angles (Appendix 2.2)
evidence: Direct statement about findings in the Li et al. dataset.

claim: The dataset of Li et al., 2022 shows the signature of volume growth in the number of mutations as a function of distance from the tumour centre.
source: the dataset of Li et al., 2022 with three-dimensional sampling also shows the signature of volume growth, both in the distribution of direction angles (Appendix 2.2) and in the number of mutations as a function of distance from the tumour centre, see Appendix 3.3.
evidence: Direct statement about findings in the Li et al. dataset.

claim: Lewinsohn et al., 2023 performed a spatio-phylogenetic analysis that found a signal of surface growth on the same data.
source: This result is at variance with a recent spatio-phylogenetic analysis performed by Lewinsohn et al., 2023, which finds a signal of surface growth on the same data.
evidence: Direct statement citing findings from another study.

claim: The findings of Lewinsohn et al., 2023 are compatible with volume growth.
source: In Appendix 3, we show that the findings of Lewinsohn et al., 2023 are compatible with volume growth
evidence: Direct statement about reanalysis of Lewinsohn et al. findings.

claim: On artificially generated volume-growth data sampled like in Li et al., the algorithm used in Lewinsohn et al., 2023 returns a spurious signal of surface growth.
source: on artificially generated volume-growth data sampled like in Li et al., the algorithm used in Lewinsohn et al., 2023 also returns a spurious signal of surface growth.
evidence: Direct statement about testing the Lewinsohn et al. algorithm on simulated data.

claim: The dispersion parameter σ quantifies the spatial dispersion of a mutation by computing the average distance of all pairs of samples carrying that mutation divided by the average distance if they were arranged in a spherical shape.
source: To quantify the spatial dispersion of a mutation, we define the dispersion parameter σ: For a given mutation, we compute the average distance of all pairs of samples carrying that mutation and divide by the average distance these cells would have if they were arranged next to one another in a spherical shape (the tightest configuration possible).
evidence: Direct definition of the dispersion parameter.

claim: Values of σ much larger than one arise when a mutation is scattered throughout the tumour with many cells that do not carry that mutation located between cells that do.
source: Values of σ much larger than one can arise when a mutation is scattered throughout the tumour, with many cells that do not carry that mutation located between cells that do.
evidence: Direct explanation of what high dispersion values indicate.

claim: The average value of the dispersion parameter in the Ling et al., 2015 whole-exome sequencing data is approximately 3.5.
source: We find an average value of the dispersion of approximately 3.5
evidence: Direct statement of measured average dispersion, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: The dispersion parameter values for specific mutations in the Ling et al., 2015 data can be as high as 9.
source: but the values for specific mutations can be much higher than that (up to 9).
evidence: Direct statement about the range of dispersion values observed.

claim: The distribution of dispersion parameters found under volume growth agrees with that in the empirical data from Ling et al., 2015 (Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics 1.13).
source: The distribution of dispersion parameters found under volume growth agrees with that in the empirical data (Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics 1.13)
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result comparing simulated and empirical data.

claim: Surface growth generates lower values of the dispersion parameter than observed in the empirical data (Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics 5.74).
source: whereas surface growth generates lower values of the dispersion parameter (Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics 5.74 indicating a poorer match with the empirical data, see Appendix 4.3 for details).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result comparing simulated and empirical data.

claim: Higher values of the dispersion parameter than expected under surface growth are found in the three-dimensional dataset of Li et al., 2022.
source: Also in the three-dimensional dataset of Li et al., 2022, we find higher values of the dispersion parameter than expected under surface growth (Appendix 4.4).
evidence: Direct statement about findings in the Li et al. dataset.

claim: Volume growth causes dispersion of mutations through tumour cells displacing one another when new cells are born and grow.
source: Volume growth offers a simple mechanism causing the dispersion of mutations: Tumour cells displace one another when new cells are born and grow.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the mechanism of dispersion under volume growth.

claim: Two cells that are initially close and share a mutation can be pushed apart by the birth and growth of adjacent cells that do not share the mutation.
source: In this way, two cells which are initially close to one another and share a mutation can be pushed apart by the birth and growth of adjacent cells that do not share the mutation.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the pushing mechanism.

claim: The further apart a pair of cells becomes, the higher the probability that they will be moved even further apart due to the motion of cells between them.
source: The further apart a pair of cells becomes, the higher the probability that they will be moved even further apart due to the motion of the increasing number of cells between them.
evidence: Direct statement about the amplification mechanism.

claim: This amplification of initially small distances leads to an instability that can generate large values of the dispersion σ.
source: This amplification of initially small distances leads to an instability that can generate the large values of the dispersion σ found both in the data of Ling et al., 2015 and in numerical simulations of the volume growth model
evidence: Direct statement linking the mechanism to observed dispersion values.

claim: Under surface growth, cells do not push each other apart, leading to lower values of the dispersion parameter.
source: On the other hand, under surface growth, cells do not push each other apart, leading to lower values of the dispersion parameter.
evidence: Direct statement contrasting surface growth with volume growth.

claim: High values of the dispersion parameter cannot arise spuriously due to positive selection.
source: Also, high values of the dispersion parameter cannot arise spuriously due to positive selection, as selected clones would enter the population later than neutral ones (given the same final frequency), and thus do not have as much time to be moved within the tumour.
evidence: Direct statement ruling out selection as a confounding factor.

claim: The dispersion of cells in a growing population via pushing is well known in tissue mechanics.
source: The dispersion of cells in a growing population via this pushing effect is well known in tissue mechanics (Ranft et al., 2010; Malmi-Kakkada et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement citing prior work on cell dispersion in tissue mechanics.

claim: Ultra-deep sequencing of multiple samples from solid tumours has found clonal mixing.
source: In the context of cancer, it provides a mechanism for the clonal mixing found by ultra-deep sequencing of multiple samples from a solid tumour (Sottoriva et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2017)
evidence: Direct statement citing studies that found clonal mixing.

claim: Clonal mixing leads to mutations that occur at high frequencies in some samples being present at low frequencies in other samples.
source: which leads to mutations that occur at high frequencies in some samples being present at low (but non-zero) frequencies in other samples.
evidence: Direct statement describing the pattern of clonal mixing.

claim: Dispersion and clonal mixing arise as a by-product of volume growth.
source: Dispersion and clonal mixing thus arise as a by-product of volume growth.
evidence: Direct statement linking dispersion and clonal mixing to volume growth.

claim: Under surface growth, a specific dispersal mechanism has been postulated to account for the observed spatial distribution of mutations.
source: This is in contrast to surface growth, where a specific dispersal mechanism has been postulated to account for the observed spatial distribution of mutations (Waclaw et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement citing prior work on surface growth models.

claim: About 75% of all mutations can be detected with only five samples from the 23 whole-exome samples of Ling et al., 2015.
source: One finds that typically about 75% of all the mutations can be detected with only five samples.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4A.

claim: When mutations present at higher frequency in other samples are removed, five samples typically contain only about one-fifth of the mutations.
source: With such mutations removed, five samples typically only contain about one-fifth of the mutations.
evidence: Direct statement about the effect of removing migrated mutations.

claim: Migration of cells makes a single sample capture a far larger share of the genetic variability than expected from its share of the sampled tumour volume.
source: Migration of cells thus makes a single sample capture a far larger share of the genetic variability than expected from its share of the sampled tumour volume
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from the analysis of mutation detection.

claim: The inferred rate of cell death from the Ling et al., 2015 data is nearly as high as the rate of birth (relative death rate 0.975 with 90% confidence interval [0.83, 0.995]).
source: We find a rate of cell death nearly as high as the rate of birth (relative death rate 0.975 with 90% confidence interval [0.83, 0.995]).
evidence: Direct statement of inferred parameter with confidence interval, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: During its early stage, the tumour was balanced nearly perfectly between growth and extinction.
source: Hence during its early stage, the tumour was balanced nearly perfectly between growth and extinction.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from the high death rate.

claim: The inferred exome-wide mutation rate μ per cell division is 0.015 with 90% confidence interval [0.002, 0.1].
source: The inferred exome-wide mutation rate μ per cell division is 0.015 with 90% confidence interval [0.002, 0.1].
evidence: Direct statement of inferred parameter with confidence interval, supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Werner et al., 2020 found low rates of cell death across many cancer data sets.
source: This result is at variance with a recent analysis based on the distribution of mutational distances between samples. Werner et al., 2020 find low rates of cell death across many cancer data sets.
evidence: Direct statement citing findings from another study.

claim: Widely different rates of cell deaths are compatible with a given distribution of pairwise distances between samples.
source: In Appendix 6, we show that this discrepancy arises because widely different rates of cell deaths are compatible with a given distribution of pairwise distances between samples.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the discrepancy with Werner et al.

claim: The tumour mutation rate was enhanced by a factor of 5 compared to healthy human fibroblasts.
source: this would mean the tumour mutation rate was enhanced by a factor of 5.
evidence: Direct statement comparing tumour and normal mutation rates.

claim: The strongest mutational signature in all three tumours is single-base-substitution signature 22 (SBS22).
source: Figure 5 shows that the strongest signature in all tumours is the single-base-substitution signature 22 (SBS22).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5.

claim: Mutational signature SBS22 has been associated with exposure to the exogenous mutagen aristolochic acid.
source: This signature has been associated with exposure to the exogenous mutagen aristolochic acid (Hoang et al., 2013)
evidence: Direct statement citing the association of SBS22 with aristolochic acid.

claim: Aristolochic acid is a herbal component used in traditional Chinese medicine.
source: aristolochic acid (Hoang et al., 2013), a herbal component used in traditional Chinese medicine.
evidence: Direct statement describing aristolochic acid.

claim: The cancer patients of Ling et al. and Li et al. lived in China.
source: (The cancer patients of the Ling et al. and Li et al. lived in China.)
evidence: Direct statement about patient location.

claim: The Li et al. tumours maintain similar mutational signatures over pseudo-time.
source: While the Li et al. tumours maintain similar mutational signatures over pseudo-time
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5.

claim: In the Ling et al. patient, exposure to aristolochic acid appears to have ceased over the course of tumour evolution.
source: we find that the exposure to aristolochic acid of the patient from Ling et al. appears to have ceased over the course of tumour evolution
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from the mutational signature analysis.

claim: Mutational signature SBS22 dominates the clonal mutations in the Ling et al. data but is absent in the subclonal mutations.
source: while the mutational signature SBS22 dominates the clonal mutations, it is absent in the subclonal mutations, see Figure 5.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5.

claim: The probability of not observing subclonal SBS22 due to sampling noise (p-value) was estimated to be less than 10^−4.
source: The probability of not observing subclonal SBS22 due to sampling noise (p-value) was estimated to be less than 10−4, see Appendix 9.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical significance.

claim: Under neutral evolution and neglecting fluctuations in clone sizes, the final frequency of a mutation that arose when a tumour consisted of N cells is given by f=1/N.
source: Under neutral evolution and neglecting fluctuations in clone sizes, the final frequency (in the entire population) of a mutation that arose when a tumour consisted of N cells is given by f=1/N (Durrett, 2013).
evidence: Direct statement citing a theoretical result.

claim: A lower limit on the frequency f corresponds to an upper limit on the population size.
source: A lower limit on the frequency f thus corresponds to an upper limit on the population size.
evidence: Direct logical inference from the relationship between frequency and population size.

claim: The mutations detected in the samples with high spatial resolution arose when the tumour consisted of about 80,000 cells.
source: We find that the mutations detected in the samples with high spatial resolution (surface growth/volume growth analysis and genetic turnover) arose when the tumour consisted of about 80,000 cells.
evidence: Direct statement of inferred population size.

claim: The mutations in the whole-exome samples used to measure the dispersion of mutations arose when the tumour size was around 7000 cells.
source: The mutations in the whole-exome samples used to measure the dispersion of mutations arose when the tumour size was around 7000 cells.
evidence: Direct statement of inferred population size.

claim: Phylogenetic comparison of samples from primary and metastatic tumours has elucidated the dynamics of metastasis.
source: on a larger spatial scale, phylogenetic comparison of samples from primary and metastatic tumours has elucidated the dynamics of metastasis (Jones et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2016; Alves et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Direct statement citing prior work on metastasis dynamics.

claim: Analyses of multiple samples from the same tumour have established intra-tumour heterogeneity.
source: Analyses of multiple samples from the same tumour have established intra-tumour heterogeneity
evidence: Direct statement about findings from multi-region sequencing studies.

claim: Neutral evolution has been found in many tumours through multi-region sampling analyses.
source: and found neutral evolution in many cases (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Sottoriva et al., 2015; Ling et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017; see Tarabichi et al., 2018 for a critique)
evidence: Direct statement citing studies that found neutral evolution.

claim: Instances of selection have been found in tumours through multi-region sampling analyses.
source: as well as instances of selection (Williams et al., 2018; Caravagna et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement citing studies that found selection.

claim: The mode of growth of a tumour affects the resulting genetic diversity of a tumour.
source: The mode of growth of a tumour affects the resulting genetic diversity of a tumour (Noble et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022).
evidence: Direct statement citing studies on the relationship between growth mode and genetic diversity.

claim: The tumour evolved under uniform volume growth with no evidence of spatial constraints leading to radially outward growth.
source: We found that the tumour evolved under uniform volume growth; there was no evidence of spatial constraints leading to radially outward growth.
evidence: Direct summary statement of main finding.

claim: A substantial turnover of cells was found with a rate of cell death comparable to the rate of cell division.
source: We also found a substantial turnover of cells with a rate of cell death comparable to the rate of cell division.
evidence: Direct summary statement of main finding.

claim: In its early stage, the tumour was balanced precariously between continued growth to macroscopic size and shrinkage.
source: Instead, in its early stage, the tumour was balanced precariously between continued growth to macroscopic size and shrinkage
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from the high death rate.

claim: A small increase in the rate of cell death or a small decrease in the growth rate would have caused the small net growth rate to become negative, possibly leading to tumour extinction.
source: A small increase in the rate of cell death, or a small decrease in the growth rate would have caused the small net growth rate to become negative, possibly even leading to the extinction of the tumour.
evidence: Direct statement about the implications of the growth-death balance.

claim: The data analysed capture the evolutionary dynamics up to 80,000 cells.
source: We estimate that the data analysed here capture the evolutionary dynamics up to 80,000 cells.
evidence: Direct statement about the temporal scope of the analysis.

claim: Increasing the genomic and spatial resolution will allow to identify mutations of lower frequency and characterize in-vivo evolution beyond the early stages.
source: Increasing the genomic and spatial resolution will allow to identify mutations of lower frequency and thus characterize the in-vivo evolution beyond the early stages.
evidence: Direct statement about future possibilities.

claim: Future techniques to sequence resected tumours at higher spatial and genomic resolution will allow to trace key later-stage evolutionary changes like angiogenesis, effects of the tumour microenvironment, or the development of genetic instability.
source: Future techniques to sequence resected tumours at higher spatial and genomic resolution than currently possible will allow to trace key later-stage evolutionary changes like angiogenesis, effects of the tumour microenvironment, or the development of genetic instability.
evidence: Direct statement about future possibilities.

claim: The distribution of direction angles is a model-independent metric that does not rely on a particular model of cell dynamics, population dynamics or sampling.
source: The distribution of direction angles is a model-independent metric, it does not rely on a particular model of cell dynamics, population dynamics or sampling.
evidence: Direct statement about the properties of the metric.

claim: The distribution of direction angles is robust against the presence of selected subclones.
source: It is also robust against the presence of selected subclones: if a subclone grows isotropically from some point, but at an elevated rate, it will contribute to a flat distribution of angles like all other clones.
evidence: Direct statement about the robustness of the metric.

claim: The samples in the Ling et al. study form a honey-comb structure because the tumour slice had been cut into four quadrants.
source: The samples form a honey-comb structure, because the tumour slice had been cut into four quadrants, see Fig S1 in Ling et al., 2015.
evidence: Direct explanation of the spatial arrangement shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An off-lattice cell-based model was used that is well-known from simulations of tissue mechanics.
source: We use an off-lattice cell-based model, well-known from simulations of tissue mechanics (Drasdo and Höhme, 2005; Van Liedekerke et al., 2019; Malmi-Kakkada et al., 2018; Metzcar et al., 2019)
evidence: Direct statement citing prior work on the modeling approach.

claim: Each tumour cell in the model is described by a sphere centered on a particular point in 3D or 2D space, as well as a genome.
source: In this model, each tumour cell is described by a sphere centered on a particular point in 3D space or 2D space, as well as a genome.
evidence: Direct description of the model.

claim: Each cell division introduces a new point adjacent to its parent in a random uniformly distributed direction.
source: Each cell division introduces a new point adjacent to its parent in a random (uniformly distributed) direction
evidence: Direct description of the model.

claim: At division, both mother and daughter cell can acquire mutations, with the number of mutations being Poisson distributed with mean μ.
source: At division both mother and daughter cell can acquire mutations, the number of mutations is Poisson distributed with mean μ.
evidence: Direct description of the mutation model.

claim: The spheres representing cells are not allowed to overlap and can push one another out of the way.
source: The spheres are not allowed to overlap and can push one another out of the way to achieve this.
evidence: Direct description of the model mechanics.

claim: The off-lattice approach differs from cellular automaton models where cells occupy discrete lattice sites.
source: This off-lattice approach differs from cellular automaton models of tumour growth, where cells occupy discrete lattice sites (Waclaw et al., 2015; Chkhaidze et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct comparison with other modeling approaches.

claim: In off-lattice models, cells can gradually push one another out of the way during growth.
source: Specifically, in off-lattice models like the one we use, cells can gradually push one another out of the way during growth, see below.
evidence: Direct statement about model behavior.

claim: The division rate b(ρ) decreases linearly from b(ρ=0)=b_0 to b(ρ=ρ_c)=0.
source: For simplicity, we consider a division rate b(ρ) which decreases in a straight line from b(ρ=0)=b0 to b(ρ=ρc)=0, see Fig. S1.
evidence: Direct description of the model with reference to figure.

claim: Setting ρ_c=∞ leads to a constant division rate for all cells, irrespective of their local density, termed volume growth.
source: Setting ρc=∞ leads to a constant division rate for all cells, irrespective of their local density. This growth mode is termed volume growth.
evidence: Direct definition of volume growth in the model.

claim: Lower values of ρ_c lead to an increased growth rate in parts of the tumour where the local density of cancer cells is low, enhancing the growth rate at the surface relative to the bulk.
source: Lower values of ρc lead to an increased growth rate in parts of the tumour where the local density of cancer cell is low, and hence enhance the growth rate at the surface of the tumour relative to the bulk of the tumour.
evidence: Direct description of how the model parameter affects growth mode.

claim: Surface growth is characterized by a ρ_c equal to the density defined by the minimal cell distance.
source: Surface growth is characterized by a ρc equal to the density defined by the minimal cell distance.
evidence: Direct definition of surface growth in the model.

claim: An infinite-sites model and a constant mutation rate per cell division were used to describe genetic changes in the tumour.
source: To describe the genetic changes in the tumour, we use an infinite-sites model and a constant mutation rate per cell division.
evidence: Direct description of the mutation model.

claim: Using off-lattice cell-based modelling, population sizes of several ten thousand cells can be simulated.
source: Using off-lattice cell-based modelling, population sizes of several ten thousand cells can be simulated, compared to billions of cells with a cellular automaton (Waclaw et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement about computational capabilities.

claim: Cellular automaton models can simulate billions of cells.
source: compared to billions of cells with a cellular automaton (Waclaw et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct comparison citing another modeling approach.
